messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tai, a 67-year-old widowed interior designer of Samoan descent, has not entered his studio in over a year. The trouble began two years ago, when two men broke into his home, bound him to a chair in a small bathroom, and ransacked the house while shouting in Arabic. For several hours he sat in that confined space, convinced he would be killed. The memory of that afternoon has never left him.

Intrusive memories strike without warning—a sudden image of the bathroom tiles, or more often the sound of shouting in Arabic from a passing car or a neighbor's television. These triggers instantly flood him with strong negative feelings: fear, horror, anger, and a deep shame that he did not fight back. His body reacts before his mind can catch up—his heart pounds, his breathing turns shallow, and he feels an urgent need to press his back against a wall where he can see the entire room. That state of hypervigilance, in turn, tends to pull forward more memories—the captors' voices, the smell of the space. When he tries to describe what happened to a friend, he often loses the thread and cannot finish, and at other times he recalls the events but feels completely numb, as if they happened to a stranger; yet even that numb recall triggers the same visceral threat response, as if his own detachment fools no part of him.

To manage the constant sense of danger, Tai has developed rigid strategies. He rehearses what to say before any social interaction, scripting each line so he can avoid feeling emotionally vulnerable. He avoids enclosed or confined spaces entirely—elevators, small restrooms, tight hallways. Most consequentially, he has stopped going to work. As an interior designer, he used to visit clients' homes and new construction sites; now the thought of entering an unfamiliar enclosed room is unbearable. These strategies, however, have a paradoxical effect. Rehearsing conversations keeps his mind fixed on potential threats, amplifying his sense of danger and keeping his body on constant alert. Avoiding work and confinement leaves him isolated at home, where the silence often gives way to auditory memories—the shouting in Arabic echoes in his head, and the memory becomes more vivid and intrusive the more he tries to shut it out.

Since the attack, Tai has lived in a state of near-constant hypervigilance. He always chooses a seat with his back to a wall, scanning the room for exits. This level of alertness makes him acutely sensitive to any sound that could be shouting, especially in a language he does not understand. A raised voice at a grocery store, a neighbor's television, a car horn—each can trigger a vivid intrusive memory, because his body is already braced for danger before his mind has even identified the source.

Tai finally sought help after a trip to the grocery store ended in a panic attack when a customer shouted to a friend across the aisle. He is terrified he will become completely housebound. He is hoping to regain the independence he lost after his wife’s death, but he is also afraid that talking about the captivity will make the memories worse—and that he might lose the only thread of control he has left.
